passage: Neutrality has a poor reputation among people who think seriously about war. To its critics it looks like a refusal to choose, a way for a small state to sit out the great moral contests of its time while others pay the price of deciding them. On this view the neutral is a free rider at best and a quiet collaborator at worst, trading with whichever side is winning and calling its caution a principle. The charge is not baseless, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what neutrality has usually been for the states that practised it with any success.

For a small country surrounded by larger ones, neutrality is less a moral posture than a strategy, and a demanding one. Its purpose is to remove the country from the calculations of its neighbours, to persuade each of them that the territory will never be used as a road or a base by the others. That persuasion does not come from declarations. It has to be earned through a long record of evenhanded conduct, through refusing favours that would look like alignment, and, above all, through an army strong enough to make occupation expensive. The neutral that cannot defend its borders is not neutral in any meaningful sense; it is simply unclaimed, and unclaimed ground in wartime is soon claimed.

Seen this way, neutrality is not passivity but a continuous effort of a particular kind. The neutral state must be ready to resist whichever side violates its frontier first, which means it must arm against all of its neighbours at once rather than against one. It must also be disciplined in peacetime, since a single treaty of friendship, a preferential trade deal or a careless remark by a minister can be read abroad as a signal of where it would stand in a crisis. Few alliances ask as much of their members as this solitary commitment asks of a country that has chosen it.

None of this guarantees success. Neutrality works only so long as the great powers judge that respecting it costs them less than violating it, and when a neutral's territory becomes essential to someone's war plans, even a well-armed and scrupulous record may count for little. Nor does the strategic defence settle every moral question; a neutral that profits handsomely from a war it claims to stand apart from invites the suspicion its critics voice. But the critics usually ask the wrong question. They ask whether neutrality is admirable, when the more useful question is whether, for a particular state in a particular place, it is the course most likely to keep that state's people out of a war they could not win.

passage: Few practices in science are defended as warmly, or examined as rarely, as anonymous peer review. A manuscript arrives at a journal, an editor sends it to two or three specialists, and their verdicts, delivered without signatures, decide whether the work enters the published record. The usual defence of the anonymity is straightforward and has real force. A young researcher asked to assess a paper by the most powerful figure in her field may hesitate to point out its flaws if her name is attached to the report, since that figure may one day sit on the committee that decides her promotion. Anonymity, on this view, is what allows candour to flow upward.

The trouble is that the same protection shelters other things as well. A referee who is quietly working on a rival theory, or whose own earlier results are contradicted by the manuscript, can recommend rejection without ever having to explain himself in public. Most referees, of course, do nothing of the kind; the difficulty is that nobody outside the editorial office can tell which ones do. Authors receive a verdict but not a reason they can contest, and readers never learn that a paper was turned away at all. A system designed to free the weak from the strong can thus end up freeing the established from scrutiny, because it is usually the established who are asked to referee, and a manuscript that challenges a reigning view is, by the nature of the case, most likely to be sent to the very people who hold that view.

It would nevertheless be wrong to infer from all this that anonymity is, in itself, the problem. What makes it dangerous is its combination with gatekeeping power. When a referee's report merely advises, when it is published alongside the paper as one reader's criticism that the authors can answer, the identity of the critic matters far less, because the criticism must persuade on its merits. When the report decides, in secret, whether anyone will read the paper at all, the absence of a name becomes the absence of accountability.

Some journals have begun to experiment along these lines, publishing papers first and attaching the referees' reports afterwards, sometimes signed and sometimes not. Such arrangements are not free of costs: they may let weak work into circulation, and they ask readers to do more of the sorting. But they reveal what the familiar arrangement conceals, namely that the case for anonymous review has always rested on an assumption about what review is for. If review exists to improve papers, a mask does little harm. If it exists to decide which papers exist, the mask deserves far more suspicion than it usually receives.

passage: Whenever a machine produces fluent language, the question returns of whether it understands what it says. Two answers dominate. One holds that understanding is shown in behaviour: if a system answers questions, follows instructions and sustains a conversation in ways we cannot distinguish from a competent person, there is nothing further we could reasonably ask of it, and to withhold the word is mere prejudice in favour of our own kind. The other holds that behaviour, however impressive, can be produced by manipulating symbols whose connection to the world the system never grasps, and that understanding requires something behind the performance, some grounding of words in perception, action or experience.

The two camps disagree about almost everything except one assumption, and that shared assumption is where the trouble lies. Both treat understanding as a single property that a system either has or lacks, so that the only task is to decide which side of the line it falls on. Yet when we attribute understanding to people we do nothing of the kind. A student may understand a theorem well enough to apply it to textbook problems but not well enough to see why it fails when one condition is dropped; a mechanic may understand an engine thoroughly in practice while being unable to explain its thermodynamics. We judge understanding by a battery of loosely connected abilities: explaining, extending to unfamiliar cases, noticing one's own mistakes, connecting what one knows to what one does. These abilities can come apart, and people possess them in very different measures.

If understanding is a cluster of this kind, the all-or-nothing question about machines is badly posed. A system may display some of the abilities to a high degree and others hardly at all; it may extend a pattern brilliantly in one domain and fail, without any sign of noticing, at a trivial variation in another. Saying that it 'really understands' flattens this profile into a verdict that tells us little, and saying that it 'merely manipulates symbols' does the same in the opposite direction. The useful work lies in mapping which abilities are present, under what conditions, and how robustly.

This proposal will not satisfy everyone. Someone who believes that understanding involves an inner experience of meaning will say that mapping abilities, however finely, leaves the essential question untouched. Perhaps it does. But that question, whatever its answer, is a question about experience, and it arises equally for any being whose inner life we cannot inspect. It should not be allowed to stand in for the more tractable question of what a system can and cannot reliably do, which is, after all, the question on which most practical decisions about such systems depend.

passage: We tend to think of the weekend as a natural feature of the calendar, as if two days of rest had always followed five of work. In fact the arrangement is fairly recent, and its history suggests that free time is not simply the absence of work but something that has to be made, defended and shaped. Before the factory, many artisans worked in bursts, labouring late into the night to finish an order and then taking a day or two off whenever it suited them; in parts of England the habit of stretching Sunday's rest into Monday was common enough to be given a mock saint's name, 'Saint Monday'.

Factory production could not tolerate this irregularity. Machines were expensive and had to run whenever the hands were present, and an employer could not plan production around workers who might drift in on Tuesday, so the long struggle over hours was therefore also a struggle over the shape of time. Workers wanted fewer hours; employers wanted predictable ones. The compromise that eventually emerged, first a half-day on Saturday and later the whole of it, gave each side part of what it sought. Workers won rest that was guaranteed rather than snatched, and employers won a workforce that turned up, sober, on Monday morning.

It would be wrong to see the outcome merely as a defeat dressed up as a victory. For most working people, guaranteed free time was a real gain, and it was won against resistance. But the weekend also changed what free time was. Leisure that had once been taken at the worker's discretion became a fixed block, the same for everyone, and a block that was the same for everyone could be sold to. Football matches, excursion trains and seaside resorts arranged themselves around Saturday afternoon and Sunday, and leisure came increasingly to mean something one went out and paid for at a scheduled time.

The lesson is not that the old irregular rhythm was better; it was often tied to poverty, to insecurity and to binges of overwork that left people exhausted. It is that arguments about working hours are never only about quantity. When people today argue over flexible schedules or a four-day week, they are reopening a question that the industrial age settled in one particular way: not merely how much time should be free, but who decides when it falls and what it is for.

passage: Tourists, it is often observed, are rarely content with what is shown to them. The monument, the parade, the dance performed on a stage in the hotel courtyard: all of these are understood to be presentations, arranged for visitors, and for that reason they seem to many travellers less real than whatever lies behind them. What the discerning visitor wants is the back region, the kitchen rather than the dining room, the village household rather than the folk show, the place where people are simply living rather than performing. Tourism, on this view, is a search for the unperformed, conducted by people whose very presence makes performance likely.

The difficulty is that the search creates its object, for once visitors will pay to see behind the scenes, behind the scenes becomes a scene. Homestays are furnished to look lived in; working kitchens are tidied and lit for the guided tour; a weaving cooperative arranges its looms so that visitors can watch the ordinary work of the day at a convenient hour. Each of these presents itself as a glimpse of the back, and each is in fact another front, built in the shape of a back. Critics of tourism have made much of this, arguing that the visitor who congratulates himself on having escaped the tourist trail has merely been led down a more expensive branch of it.

The criticism is accurate about the arrangements and, I think, mistaken about the tourists. It assumes that they are dupes who believe they have found the real thing and would be dismayed to learn otherwise. Many are nothing of the kind: asked directly, a good number will say that of course the homestay was prepared for them, that of course the cooperative works differently when no one is watching. What they value is not the illusion of having seen the unstaged but the experience of being admitted, of being received as a guest rather than seated as a spectator, and that experience is not falsified by the knowledge that it was arranged. A theatre audience is not deceived merely because it knows the actors are acting.

If there is a cost in all this, it falls elsewhere. Every back region that is opened to visitors must be replaced by another, further back, where the hosts can live without being watched, and in places where tourism is the main source of income, that retreat can go a long way. The family that rents out its courtyard confines its own life to a back room; the village that stages its festival for visitors holds the version that matters to it in the off season, or not at all. The more successfully a community sells access to its private life, the less private life it has left to sell, and the less it has left to keep for itself.

The usual question about staged authenticity is whether the tourist is being cheated. That question flatters the tourist by placing his experience at the centre of the moral picture, and it is in any case usually answered in his favour, since he generally receives what he knowingly pays for. The harder question concerns the hosts, and it is not whether they are deceiving anyone but how much of their lives they can afford to keep out of view. A tourism that respected its hosts would measure itself not by how much it manages to reveal but by how much it is content to leave alone.

passage: It is often said that forgiveness must be earned. On this view, the wrongdoer must first acknowledge what he did, express remorse and, where possible, make amends; only then is the victim in a position to forgive, and to forgive earlier would be to excuse the wrong or to collude in pretending that it did not matter. The view has an attractive moral seriousness. It refuses to let forgiveness become a soft word for forgetting, and it insists that wrongs make demands on the people who commit them.

But the view also has an awkward consequence, for it puts the victim's moral recovery in the hands of the person who harmed her. A woman wronged by a former friend who has since died, or who simply refuses to admit anything, would on this account be permanently barred from forgiving. She could stop thinking about the wrong, or decide that it no longer troubled her, but she could not forgive, because the conditions for forgiveness depend on someone else's change of heart. It is strange to make one of the most personal acts a person can perform conditional on the cooperation of the one person least likely to give it.

A better account distinguishes between what forgiveness is and what makes it fitting. To forgive is to give up resentment and the claim to repayment while continuing to judge that the act was wrong. Understood in this way, forgiveness does not excuse anything, since the judgement of wrong remains in place. What an apology does is make forgiveness easier and, often, more appropriate, because it removes the reason that resentment had for persisting: the wrongdoer who sincerely apologises has, in effect, joined the victim in condemning what he did. Without an apology, forgiveness remains possible, but it is a gift rather than a response, and it is offered for the victim's reasons rather than the wrongdoer's.

This is not to say that unconditional forgiveness is always admirable. Someone who forgives every injury at once, before she has even registered that she was wronged, may be showing not generosity but a lack of self-respect, and forgiveness that comes too easily can signal that the forgiver does not believe she was owed anything. A person who is slighted again and again by the same colleague, and who forgives each slight as though nothing had happened, may also be teaching the colleague that such slights cost him nothing, which serves neither of them. The point is only that apology is one route to forgiveness rather than its gatekeeper.

passage: Why should anyone help a stranger they will never meet again? Kindness between relatives can be explained by shared interests, and kindness between neighbours by the expectation that favours will be returned. But much of human cooperation takes place between people who are neither kin nor repeat partners: the traveller who returns a lost wallet, the customer who corrects an undercharge. One influential answer is that such acts are paid for not by the person helped but by everyone who comes to hear of them. If people prefer to help those who have a record of helping others, then a good reputation is an asset, and an act of generosity towards a stranger is an investment in it. Biologists call this arrangement indirect reciprocity.

The idea has an obvious weakness, and its defenders have had to work hard to answer it. Reputation is only as useful as the information that carries it. In a small band where everyone watches everyone, deeds are seen and remembered; in a large society most of them go unwitnessed. Here language does decisive work. Gossip, often dismissed as idle, is the channel through which a person's conduct becomes known to people who never saw it, and a great deal of everyday conversation consists of exactly this exchange of judgements about absent third parties. Without such talk, indirect reciprocity could hardly operate beyond the scale of a village.

A subtler problem concerns the judgements themselves. Suppose I refuse to help someone who is known to cheat. Should observers count my refusal against me? If they do, anyone who withholds help from cheats will be punished for it, and cheating becomes safer. If they do not, observers must keep track not only of what people did but of whom they did it to and why. Models of indirect reciprocity suggest that cooperation is far more stable under the second, more demanding standard, which may help explain why people care so much about motives and context when they assess one another's behaviour.

It would be too much to say that reputation explains all cooperation among strangers. People sometimes behave generously in conditions of genuine anonymity, and laboratory attempts to show that subtle cues of being watched, such as pictures of eyes, make people more generous have produced mixed results. A defender of the reputational account can reply that habits formed in a world where anonymity was rare are not switched off merely because a particular situation happens to be unobserved. That reply is plausible, but it shifts the explanation from calculation to disposition, and it should be acknowledged as a shift. What survives is a narrower and more defensible claim: that the expectation of being talked about is one of the main forces that make large-scale cooperation possible, and that it works only as well as the talk is accurate.

options.D: allows relatives and neighbours to coordinate the return of favours that they owe to one another.

passage: Few proposals in environmental policy provoke as much unease as the suggestion that nature should be given a price. To put a figure in money on a wetland, a forest or a population of pollinating insects seems to many people a category mistake, as though one were to ask what a friendship is worth in rupees. Critics worry that once a forest has a price it can be sold, and that the language of valuation quietly concedes the very thing it was meant to resist: that everything can be exchanged for money.

Defenders of valuation reply that the choice is not between pricing nature and refusing to. Every decision to drain a marsh for housing, or to leave it alone, already implies a valuation; it merely leaves the valuation unstated. When a planning authority approves a road through a forest because the time saved by drivers is worth a stated sum, and counts the forest as worth nothing because no one has put a figure on it, the forest has in effect been priced at zero. Making the value explicit, on this view, does not turn nature into a commodity but protects it from being treated as free. A wetland that absorbs floodwater does work that would otherwise require embankments and pumps, and the cost of those replacements is a reasonable, if rough, guide to what the wetland does for the town beside it.

This reply seems to me largely right, but only within limits that its enthusiasts tend to forget. Valuation in money is a tool for comparing small changes: whether to drain this marsh or that one, whether to widen a road by a lane or route it elsewhere. It answers the question of what a little more or a little less of something is worth, given that most of it remains. It is far less suited to valuing whole systems on which economic life itself depends. To ask what all the pollinators in the world are worth is not like asking what one orchard's bees are worth and multiplying by the number of orchards. If the pollinators were gone, the prices used in the calculation, of fruit, of land, of labour, would themselves be different, and the figure would describe a world that no longer exists. Very large totals for the value of nature's services, however striking, should therefore be read as rhetoric rather than as accounts.

The practical lesson is to use valuation where it is strong and to set limits where it is weak. For decisions at the margin, an explicit figure is better than an implicit zero. For losses that would be large, irreversible or system-wide, a rule that simply forbids them, such as a minimum area of forest or a floor on water quality, may serve better than any price, because the price would become meaningless at exactly the point where it mattered most.

passage: Few words in urban debate do as much damage as 'density', largely because it is used, often by the same speaker within a single argument, to mean two quite different things. In its technical sense density is a ratio: the number of people, or of dwellings, on a given area of land. In ordinary speech it usually means something closer to crowding, the experience of too many people in too little room: a family of six in a single room, a queue that spills into the road, a train in which nobody can turn round. The two can occur together, but they need not, and treating them as one has shaped a century of planning.

Consider two districts with the same number of residents per hectare. In the first, people live in tall apartment buildings with generous flats, set among parks and wide streets. In the second, the same population is packed into low houses, several households to a building, with lanes too narrow for a cart. On a map of density the districts are identical; to anyone who lives in them they could hardly be more different. Conversely, a scattered agricultural village, where extended families share a single dwelling, can be acutely crowded indoors while being nearly empty by the hectare. Density, in short, describes land; crowding describes the conditions of daily life.

The confusion has a history. The diseases that ravaged industrial cities in the nineteenth century were widely blamed on density, and reformers responded by trying to spread people out. Yet what made those cities so lethal was a combination of overcrowded rooms, contaminated water and absent sewers, and where water and drains were improved, death rates in dense districts fell even though the districts often remained dense. The reformers were right that something was wrong; they were imprecise about what it was, and the imprecision outlived them, surviving in zoning codes and building regulations long after the sanitary conditions that had justified it had disappeared.

This is not to say that density is costless. Many people living close together compete for parks, school places and quiet, and a district can feel oppressive even when no room in it is overcrowded. Perception counts, and planners who dismiss it will find their schemes resented. But the remedies differ. Crowding is relieved by more floor space per person and by services; the costs of density are managed by design, by open space and by the quality of the street. A policy that caps density in the name of relieving crowding may achieve neither, pushing people into fewer and more crowded rooms, or out to the edge of the city.

passage: Economists who agree that carbon emissions should carry a price often disagree, sometimes heatedly, about how the price should be set. One camp prefers a tax: the government announces a charge per tonne of emissions and leaves firms to decide how much to cut. The other prefers a cap with tradable permits: the government fixes the total quantity of emissions allowed, issues permits for that amount, and lets trading among firms determine what a permit costs. In a world without uncertainty the two would be equivalent. Any cap implies some price at which permits would trade, and any tax implies some level to which emissions would fall; a regulator who knew the costs of abatement could reach the same outcome by either route.

The difference appears once we admit that no one knows those costs in advance. A tax fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain: if cutting emissions proves harder than expected, firms will pay the tax and emit more than was planned. A cap fixes the quantity and leaves the price uncertain: if cutting proves harder, permit prices will climb, perhaps steeply. Which uncertainty is more tolerable depends on the shape of the damage. If each additional tonne does roughly the same harm as the last, a fixed price tracks the damage well and a volatile price merely adds cost. If harm accelerates sharply past some threshold, a fixed quantity matters more than a stable price. Because the harm from carbon depends on the stock accumulated in the atmosphere over decades rather than on any single year's emissions, many economists conclude that year-to-year overshoots matter little and that a tax, or something that behaves like one, is the better instrument.

Advocates of trading reply that this argument, persuasive in the seminar room, neglects politics. A cap states its environmental goal openly, which can make it easier to defend, and the free allocation of permits to affected industries, though it hands them a windfall, has often been the price of getting a scheme adopted at all. A tax, by contrast, announces a cost to every voter and invites a fresh campaign against it with every scheduled rise.

The more telling fact is that, in practice, the two designs have drifted towards each other. Trading schemes have acquired price floors, to keep permits from becoming nearly worthless when demand falls, and price ceilings, to stop them from spiking; taxes have been given scheduled increases linked to emissions targets. The resulting hybrids are neither pure price nor pure quantity. This convergence suggests that the long debate was, in part, a debate about labels. What decides whether a carbon price works is less whether it is called a tax or a cap than whether it is high enough, broad enough in what it covers, and credible enough that firms invest on the expectation that it will last.

passage: The word from which the essay takes its name once meant an attempt or a trial, the act of testing something by weighing it, and the form has never quite outgrown that sense. An essay, in its original spirit, is not the report of a conclusion already reached but the record of a mind trying a thought to see whether it will bear weight. It may change direction halfway through, concede more than it intended, or end with a question sharper than the one it started with. These are not lapses. They are the form doing what it was invented to do, and the reader of such an essay is permitted to overhear a mind in conversation with itself rather than merely to receive the outcome of that conversation.

It is worth noticing how far the essay most people now encounter has moved from this. The essay that is taught in schools and demanded in universities opens with a thesis, marshals evidence in its favour, dispatches objections and restates the thesis at the close. It is, in effect, a miniature treatise, and its virtues are those of the treatise: clarity of claim, economy of proof, a structure the reader can grasp in advance. These are real virtues, and there are good reasons to teach them, not least that a writer who cannot state a claim plainly is in no position to test it. But the result is that a generation of writers has learned to regard any movement of thought within a piece of writing as a defect of planning, something to be removed in revision so that the finished text looks as though its conclusion had been visible from the first sentence.

What is lost is not merely a style. The provisional essay offers something the treatise structurally cannot: a view of how a conclusion is reached, including the paths that were tried and abandoned. A reader who watches a writer test an idea against an example, find that it fails, and adjust it, learns not only where the writer arrived but how much the arrival cost and what it excluded. She is reminded, too, that the conclusion was reached by someone who could have been wrong and who knows it. The treatise presents its conclusion as if it were the only place the evidence could lead; the essay, by showing the alternatives it passed through, leaves the reader better placed to disagree. In this sense its apparent modesty is a form of candour about the limits of its own claims.

The same candour explains the essayist's much criticised first person. The 'I' of the essay is often taken for self-display, and sometimes it is exactly that. More often it marks the scope of a claim: this is how the matter looks from here, to someone with this experience, and the reader is invited to test it against her own. The impersonal voice of the treatise, by contrast, claims a standpoint from nowhere in particular, and so makes its claims harder to locate and therefore harder to contest. Its objectivity is sometimes real, but it is always also a manner, and a manner can be adopted by writers whose claims have not earned it.

None of this licenses formlessness. Provisionality is easily counterfeited, and the meandering essay that circles its subject without ever risking a claim is as familiar as the rigid one, and less useful. A thought cannot be tested unless it is first stated with enough definiteness to fail. A genuine attempt is one that might not succeed, and an essay that cannot fail because it never claims anything has not attempted anything at all. The essay at its best is therefore not the opposite of argument but argument conducted in the open, where the reader can see each step taken and judge for herself whether it holds.

passage: When a population of elephants recovers, the news is usually reported as a conservation triumph, and in an important sense it is one. But the recovery is experienced very differently at the edge of the forest. For a farming household whose maize or paddy lies along an elephant's route, a single night's visit can destroy a season's income, and the danger is not only to crops: people walking home after dark, or guarding fields from makeshift platforms, are injured and sometimes killed. The benefits of a thriving elephant population are spread thinly across a nation, or across the world; its costs are concentrated on a few villages.

Discussions of the problem often frame it as one of attitudes. Farmers who retaliate, it is said, need to be taught to value wildlife, and coexistence is presented as a disposition that can be cultivated through awareness campaigns. There is something to this, since tolerance of wild animals varies a great deal between communities and is shaped by tradition as well as by loss. Yet to treat hostility as ignorance is to misread it. A farmer who has lost three harvests to elephants may understand their ecological importance perfectly well and still be unable to afford them.

The more honest framing is distributive. Coexistence is not a state of mind but an arrangement about who bears which costs. Compensation schemes acknowledge this in principle, but in practice they are often slow, demand paperwork that poor households struggle to complete, and pay for the market value of a damaged crop while ignoring the sleepless nights, the children kept from school to guard fields and the fear that hangs over every harvest. A scheme that pays a fraction of the loss, a year late, does not shift the burden; it documents it.

Practical deterrents have their place. Some communities have experimented with fences hung with beehives, which elephants tend to avoid, or with repellents made from chilli and with networks that warn villages of approaching herds, and where these work they reduce losses at modest cost. But deterrents move the problem as often as they solve it, pushing elephants onto the next village's fields. The underlying question remains political: whether the wider society that values elephants is willing to pay, promptly and in full, those who live beside them. Until it is, appeals for tolerance ask the poorest people in the landscape to subsidise everyone else's enjoyment of a recovered species.

passage: Any decision whose costs and benefits are spread over time requires some way of comparing what happens now with what happens later, and the standard device is the discount rate. A benefit expected in a year is counted as worth somewhat less than the same benefit today; one expected in ten years, less again; and so on, at a compounding rate. Within a single human life, and over horizons of a few decades, the practice is largely uncontroversial. Its consequences become startling only when the horizon stretches across centuries. At a rate of five per cent a year, a harm that will occur two hundred years from now is valued today at a tiny fraction of one per cent of its full size, so that a policy which spared our descendants a catastrophe would barely register against even modest present costs. Whether we owe the future anything substantial thus turns, in practice, on a number that is usually set by technical convention.

It helps to separate the reasons that have been given for discounting, because they do not stand or fall together. One is pure time preference: the view that well-being simply matters less the later it occurs. Another appeals to growth. If future people will be considerably richer than we are, then a given sum of money, or a given quantity of goods, will make less difference to their lives than it would to ours, much as a rupee means less to a wealthy person than to a poor one. A third appeals to uncertainty: the further away an outcome, the less sure we can be that it will happen at all, or that there will be anyone for it to happen to.

Pure time preference is the weakest of these, at least when it is applied across generations. A person who prefers a pleasure today to a larger one next year may be imprudent, but the impatience is his own and so are its costs. To discount the well-being of people not yet born merely because they will be born later is a different matter: it is to treat a position in time as a reason for counting someone's suffering as less, in just the way that it would be indefensible to count suffering as less because it occurs in a distant country. The growth argument is more respectable, because it does not deny the equal standing of future people; it says only that the same resources will do them less good. But it is respectable only on its own assumptions. It presupposes that the future will in fact be richer, which is precisely what is in doubt if the harm in question is severe enough to undermine prosperity, and it applies only to losses for which wealth can compensate. A flooded coastline or an extinct species is not made good by a larger economy, and to discount such losses at the rate at which consumption grows is to treat them as though they could be bought back.

The argument from uncertainty deserves more sympathy than critics of discounting usually allow it. It is reasonable to give some weight to the possibility that there will be no future people at all, and a small discount for that possibility is defensible. But the rate this argument supports is far lower than the rates commonly used, and it has nothing to say about harms we are confident will occur. What emerges from these distinctions is that the choice of a discount rate is not the technical matter it is often taken to be. Each component encodes a substantive view: about whether time itself diminishes moral standing, about how confident we are in continued growth, about which losses money can repair. A rate presented as a neutral parameter is, in effect, a verdict on what the present owes to the future, reached without the argument such a verdict requires.

passage: Popular advice about habits tends to treat them as a contest of will. Bad habits persist, on this account, because people lack the resolve to stop, and good ones fail to form because people give up too soon. The remedy is accordingly motivational: set firmer goals, remind yourself why they matter, and try harder. This view has the appeal of moral simplicity, since it locates every failure in a lack of character and every success in effort, and it is repeated in a great deal of well-meant advice. The trouble with this picture is that it misdescribes what a habit is. A habit is not a desire that has grown strong but a response that has become attached to a context, so that the context itself, rather than any present intention, sets the behaviour going.

Consider someone who checks her phone each time she sits down on the morning train. At first the action may have been chosen, perhaps as a way of passing an otherwise idle part of the trip, but after hundreds of repetitions it no longer needs choosing. The seat, the motion of the carriage and the familiar stretch of the journey are enough to bring the hand to the pocket, and she may find the phone in her hand before she has formed any wish to look at it. Asking her to resolve more firmly misses the point, since resolve is not what produces the act. The cue is.

If this is right, the most effective way to change a habit is often to change the circumstances that trigger it, not to strengthen the will that opposes it. Putting the phone in a bag rather than a pocket, sitting in a different carriage, or giving the first minutes of the journey to some specific task all interrupt the link between cue and response. Each of these requires a single decision rather than a renewed act of resistance every morning, which is precisely why such changes tend to outlast good intentions. It is often observed that people find it easier to alter their routines after moving house or changing jobs, and the account explains why: the old cues have simply disappeared, and with them much of the pressure to repeat old behaviour.

Two cautions are in order, however, if the argument is not to be pushed further than it can go. First, not every repeated behaviour is a habit in this sense; some acts are repeated because the person goes on wanting the result each time, and for these, motivation does matter. Second, the power of context cuts both ways. The same disruption that frees someone from an unwanted routine can dissolve a welcome one, which is why a regular exercise habit so often lapses after a move. Willpower is not irrelevant, then, but it is a poor tool for a job that the environment, suitably arranged, performs more cheaply and more reliably.

passage: Conservation has always had favourites. Appeals for money are illustrated with tigers, pandas, whales and elephants, animals with large eyes, recognisable faces and a reputation for grandeur, and rarely with a beetle, a freshwater mussel or a lichen. Critics have long complained that this distorts priorities. If donors give to what they find beautiful, the argument runs, then most of the living world, which is small, drab or simply invisible, will be neglected, and the species most in need of help will be the least likely to receive it. The objection is not merely aesthetic. Insects, fungi and the small organisms of soil and water do much of the work that keeps ecosystems running, yet they attract only a tiny share of public concern.

The complaint has force, but it is weaker than it first appears, because a charismatic animal rarely receives protection on its own. A large predator needs a large area, and the forest or grassland that is protected for its sake also shelters thousands of less appealing species that no donor would have paid to save directly. In this sense the famous animal works as a kind of advertisement for an entire landscape. The money is raised in the name of one face, but it is spent, at least in part, on soil, water and cover that serve everything living there.

The defence holds only up to a point, however. Some of the most threatened organisms live in habitats that no charismatic animal shares: a single cave, a spring, a patch of chalk grassland, the gravel bed of one river. Protecting a tiger reserve will do nothing for them. Moreover, money given in the name of a famous animal is sometimes spent on that animal directly, on breeding programmes, tracking collars or patrols against poachers, rather than on the wider habitat, and in such cases the advertising argument does not apply at all. A donor who pays for a radio collar has helped one tiger, and perhaps the scientists who follow it, but not the river below the reserve.

The sensible conclusion is neither to abandon flagship species nor to treat them as a complete strategy. They are a tool for raising attention and money, and a useful one. But a conservation movement that allowed the tastes of donors to draw its map of priorities would leave large gaps, and those gaps would fall precisely where the most unfamiliar forms of life are found. Some part of the effort has to be directed by need rather than by appeal, even when need comes in the shape of a mussel.

passage: In the 1890s the British psychologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan proposed a rule for interpreting animal behaviour that has shaped the study of animal minds ever since. In paraphrase, it says that we should not explain an animal's action as the product of a higher mental faculty if it can be explained as the product of a lower one. The rule was a response to a real problem. Much of what then passed for evidence about animal intelligence consisted of anecdotes sent in by pet owners and naturalists, in which dogs reasoned, cats planned and birds grieved, and in which the observer's own feelings were read into whatever the animal happened to do. Against this habit, Morgan's canon was a discipline: before crediting a creature with insight, ask whether trial and error, habit or simple association would account for what you saw.

As a corrective, the canon did its work well. It pushed the field towards controlled observation and towards explanations that could be tested, and it is partly responsible for the expectation that claims about animal cognition must now survive experiments designed to rule out simpler accounts. But a rule that is useful against one error can become an error of its own when it is applied without thought. Over the following century the canon hardened, in many hands, into a presumption that the lowest available explanation is always to be preferred, whatever the animal and whatever the evidence.

The trouble with that presumption is that it is not as neutral as it looks. It treats 'lower' as if it meant 'simpler' and 'simpler' as if it meant 'more probably true', and neither equation holds in general. An explanation in terms of association may require positing a long and improbable history of exactly the right rewards, while an explanation in terms of a modest capacity to represent what another animal can see may be the more economical of the two. Evolution complicates the picture further. If a chimpanzee and a human behave alike in similar circumstances, the assumption that the behaviour rests on similar mechanisms is, given their close kinship, arguably the simpler hypothesis; to insist on a different and lower mechanism for the chimpanzee alone is to multiply explanations, not to reduce them.

There is also a question of cost. The canon guards against one kind of mistake, crediting animals with capacities they lack, and is silent about the opposite mistake, denying them capacities they have. Both mistakes are real, and the second is not obviously the less harmful, especially where the capacities in question include the ability to suffer. An investigator who refuses on principle to credit a dog with fear until every leaner account has been excluded will seldom be caught overstating anything, but she may spend a career understating what is in front of her. A principle that treats one error as serious and the other as negligible is not a principle of caution; it is a bias that happens to look like one.

None of this is a case for returning to the anecdote. Morgan himself appears to have intended his rule as a guard against careless inference rather than as a ban on crediting animals with higher faculties when there is independent evidence for them. The better successor to the canon is not its opposite but a symmetrical standard: state the rival hypotheses, rich and lean alike, and design observations that would tell them apart. Simplicity then becomes something to be argued for in each case, rather than a verdict delivered in advance.

passage: Many societies have set aside days on which the ordinary order is turned upside down. In the Roman Saturnalia, masters are said to have waited on their slaves at table; in parts of medieval Europe, junior clergy elected a mock bishop and parodied the liturgy; in countless village festivals men dress as women, children give orders to adults, and the powerful are mocked in songs that would be punished at any other time of year. Such festivals of inversion have long puzzled those who study them, because they seem to put the most fundamental arrangements of a society at risk for the sake of a few days of licence.

Two explanations have dominated. The first, often called the safety valve theory, holds that inversion protects the order it mocks. Resentments that accumulate under hierarchy are released in a bounded, harmless form, and when the festival ends everyone returns to their place, relieved and more willing to stay there. The second reverses the judgement. On this view, the festival gives people a glimpse of a world arranged otherwise, keeps alive the memory that rank is not natural, and so contains the seed of real defiance. Supporters of each view can point to cases. Rulers have tolerated and even funded such festivals, which suggests they found them useful; they have also banned them, which suggests they found them dangerous, and on a few occasions a carnival has indeed turned into a riot.

What both explanations share is the assumption that the meaning of inversion is fixed by its form, so that one need only decide, once and for all, whether turning the world upside down conserves it or threatens it. The historical record does not support so tidy a choice, since the same festival, with the same masks and the same songs, has been a harmless frolic in one decade and the occasion of an uprising in the next. The difference lay not in the ritual but in its circumstances: a bad harvest, a disputed tax, a quarrel between factions of the elite that made the mockery of one of them useful to the other. Inversion, in other words, does not carry its own political charge; it takes one from the situation into which it is performed.

The safety valve theory has a further weakness that is easy to overlook because its central image is so vivid. It pictures discontent as a kind of pressure that builds up in a closed vessel and can be let off in measured bursts. There is little reason to think that resentment, which is attached to particular injuries and particular persons, behaves like steam that can be vented without residue; people who have mocked their masters for a day do not obviously feel less aggrieved afterwards, and they may feel more entitled to their grievance for having heard it voiced aloud by a crowd. The image persuades because it is mechanical, not because anyone has observed the mechanism.

A more promising account starts from a simpler observation. To turn a world upside down, one must first show which way up it is. The mock bishop presupposes a real one; the servant who gives orders for a day makes plain who gives them on every other day. Inversion is thus a vivid lesson in hierarchy, and in that sense it does teach the order it reverses. But the lesson cuts both ways, since a ranking that can be so easily reversed in play is shown to be a convention rather than a fact of nature. Which of these lessons is learned depends, again, on what else is happening. That is an unsatisfying conclusion only for those who wanted the festival to have a single meaning.

passage: Discussion of whether photographs can be trusted has long been dominated by the fear of manipulation. Early critics worried about staged scenes and retouched negatives; later ones about software that can add a figure to a crowd or remove one from a podium without leaving a trace visible to the eye. These worries are reasonable, and the tools that prompt them have become more powerful. But they direct attention to the least interesting way in which a photograph can mislead, and in doing so they leave the more ordinary and more pervasive problem almost untouched.

Consider an unaltered photograph of a crowded square taken during a demonstration. Every figure in it was really there, standing exactly where the picture shows. The image is, in the narrow sense, entirely truthful. Yet it cannot tell us whether the square was full or whether the photographer stood at the one corner where people had gathered; whether the moment captured was typical of the afternoon or its single tense minute; whether the raised fists at the front belonged to protesters or to the counter-demonstration across the road. A photograph is accurate about what falls inside its frame and wholly silent about what falls outside it, and the frame is chosen by someone.

This is why the manipulation debate can produce a false sense of security. A viewer who has learned to check for doctored pixels may conclude that an image which passes the check is reliable, when the check has said nothing about selection, timing or framing. An honest photograph can support a dishonest story as easily as a forged one can, and often more easily, since it will survive the very scrutiny that exposes a forgery.

None of this makes photographs worthless as evidence. It means that their evidential value lies less in the single image than in its surroundings: the caption that states when and where it was taken, the other frames from the same roll or memory card, the identity and record of the person who took it, the existence of independent pictures of the same event. A photograph considered alone is a fragment that can be fitted into many stories. A photograph considered with these supports begins to narrow the stories it can serve. The question to ask of an image, then, is not only whether it has been altered but what would have to be true of everything around it for it to mean what it is said to mean.

passage: A curious feature of the market for retro goods is how many of their buyers are too young to remember the originals. Record players styled like those of the nineteen-sixties, cameras that imitate the look of early film models, soft drinks reissued in the bottles of half a century ago: these sell briskly to people for whom the period they evoke is something seen in old films rather than lived. Whatever such buyers are nostalgic for, it cannot be their own past, and any explanation of the trade has to begin from that awkward fact.

The usual explanation is that they are being fooled, that advertisers have invented a golden age and sold it back to a generation with no means of checking. There is something in this, but it misreads what the buyer is after. Nostalgia has always been less a memory than a mood, a way of expressing dissatisfaction with the present by furnishing it with an imagined contrast against which its deficiencies become visible. The retro object does not claim to restore the past; it offers a small, ownable piece of a world that seems slower, sturdier and easier to understand than the one its owner actually lives in. That such a world never quite existed matters less than the fact that the feeling it answers is real.

What is striking is how carefully the past is edited in the process. The reissued record player has a socket for a phone; the vintage-look camera stores its pictures on a memory card and adds the scratches digitally. The inconveniences that made the originals what they were, the waiting, the expense, the fragility, are removed, and only the surface is kept. Retro design is in this sense the opposite of preservation: it keeps the look of an earlier time while discarding the conditions that gave the look its meaning.

None of this need be a cause for scorn. Some revived products are genuinely better made than the disposable goods they replaced, and a taste for the durable, in an economy organised around rapid obsolescence, is not foolish. But it is worth being clear about what is being bought. The buyer of a retro radio is not recovering a lost way of life; he is purchasing a token of his unease with his own, and the market is happy to supply as many such tokens as that unease will bear.

passage: It is often said that overconfidence is the most pervasive of the biases, the one from which many of the others draw their strength. The claim is repeated so often that it is easy to miss how much it conceals. 'Overconfidence' names at least three different things, and they do not always travel together. Treating them as one has made the phenomenon seem both more universal and more mysterious than it is.

The first is overestimation: believing that one has performed, or will perform, better than one actually does. The second is overplacement: believing that one is better than other people. The third, which receives less public attention, is overprecision: excessive certainty that one's beliefs are accurate, shown when people asked for a range they are ninety per cent sure contains some true value give ranges that contain it far less often than that. These sound like variations on a single vanity, but they come apart in revealing ways. On tasks that are easy, people tend to underestimate how well they have done, even as they place themselves above others; on tasks that are very hard, the pattern reverses, and many people will rate themselves below average at, say, juggling or composing verse while still overestimating their own scores.

What explains such reversals is less a desire to think well of oneself than the way information is distributed. People usually know more about their own performance than about other people's, so their judgements of others are pulled toward a vague middle. When a task is hard, they correctly sense that they did poorly but assume that others did less badly; when it is easy, the opposite. A good deal of what looks like ego, in other words, is a predictable consequence of reasoning from imperfect information about the people with whom one is being compared.

Overprecision is different. It shows no comparable tendency to reverse, appearing on easy and hard questions, among novices and among specialists, and it is the form that does most harm in planning, where projects are budgeted against ranges too narrow to include what actually happens. It is also the form that most resists exhortation: telling forecasters to be humble rarely widens their intervals much. More promising are procedures that change the question, such as asking people to assign probabilities to several ranges in turn, so that the possibility of an outcome far from their best guess must be considered explicitly rather than waved away. The lesson is not that confidence is good or bad but that a single word has been doing the work of three, and that each of the three needs its own diagnosis.
